title: How I envy him
translation: When Tamekane, the former counsellor who had become a monk, was arrested, soldiers surrounded him and marched him off to the shogunate's headquarters at Rokuhara. Suketomo saw them go past near Ichijō. "How I envy him!" he said. "If you're going to live at all, that's the memory to take with you."
original: {為兼|ためかね}{大納言|だいなごん}{入道|にふだう}めしとられて、{武士|もののふ}ども{打|う}ち{囲|かこ}みて、{六波羅|ろくはら}へ{率|ゐ}て{行|ゆ}きければ、
{資朝卿|すけともきやう}、{一条|いちでう}わたりにてこれを{見|み}て、「あな{羨|うらやま}し。{世|よ}にあらむおもひで、かくこそ{有|あ}らまほしけれ。」とぞいはれける。
literal: When Tamekane, the Major Counsellor who had taken vows, was arrested, and the warriors surrounded him and took him to Rokuhara,
Lord Suketomo saw this around Ichijō and said, 'Ah, how enviable. As a memory of having been in the world, this is how one would like it to be.'

notes.text: Kyōgoku Tamekane (1254–1332), a leading poet and a former Major Counsellor ({大納言|だいなごん}) who had taken vows ({入道|にふだう}). His Kyōgoku school of poetry was the great rival of the Nijō school, to which Kenkō belonged (see the note on section 14). He was arrested by the shogunate twice. This is the second time, in 1315; he was exiled to Tosa the next year and never came back to the capital.
Rokuhara, in the east of Kyoto, was the seat of the Kamakura shogunate's officials in the capital, who watched over the court. Being taken there meant the shogunate was dealing with you.
{率|ゐ}る: 'to lead, take along'. The modern {率|ひき}いる is a different verb with the same kanji.
Hino Suketomo, as in section 152. Nine years after this scene, he was himself arrested by the shogunate (1324) and later exiled. The text does not mention it.

notes.quote: 世にあらむおもひで、かくこそ有らまほしけれ
notes.text: おもひで: 'a memory', something to look back on. まほし: 'would like'. こそ … けれ again. Suketomo does not pity a man led away by soldiers: he envies him.
いはれ: the respectful れ, 'he said'. ぞ … ける: ぞ needs the attributive form, so けり becomes ける.
